newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel and PLO finally agree Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel and PLO finally agree Hebron deal.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat sealed a U.S.-brokered accord on Hebron on Wednesday and agreed on a timeframe for further Israeli pullbacks in the West Bank.

Negotiators initialled the deal behind closed doors on the border between Israel and Gaza at a late-night summit between the two leaders, ending months of arduous talks that strained to breaking point relations between the uneasy peace partners.

Chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas told Reuters the deal requires Israel to withdraw its troops from 80 percent of Hebron within 10 days and implement the first of three subsequent West Bank redeployments by March 7.

"We are glad we have finalised the Hebron deal. It is the first agreement we have signed with the Likud. We hope this will be the beginning of more deals with this government," said Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen.

Israel's cabinet and the Palestinian Authority will meet separately later on Wednesday to approve the deal. Netanyahu planned to seek parliamentary ratification on Thursday after getting his ministers behind the deal.
Israel Radio predicted the cabinet would approve the accord by a vote of 11 to 6.
Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said one of the most important achievements for Israel was a letter of guarantees to Netanyahu from outgoing U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
Naveh told Israel Radio the letter stated that Israel would define the depth of the three additional West Bank pullbacks due to end, according to the Israel-PLO deal, by mid-1998.
"It is a most important thing...it shows U.S. recognition of Israel's security concerns directly related to these redeployments," Naveh said.
"I believe that the majority of Israeli cabinet ministers will be impressed by these things and the agreement will be approved," Naveh said.
By sealing the Hebron deal Netanyahu did what he and his right-wing Likud party said they would never do -- cede part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.

"I think it is a very sad moment, for the world, for the country, for the city," said Hebron settler leader Noam Arnon. "Arafat, who is still managing a terror organisation, signed an agreement with Netanyahu who wrote a book against terrorism."

PLO officials have acknowledged a 1995 interim deal with Israel did not specify the scope of the three pullbacks but they have said they believed 87 to 90 percent of the West Bank and Gaza would be under Palestinian rule after the third phase.
Some 130,000 Jewish settlers live in the two areas, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war and home to some two million Palestinians.

The depth of the three redeployments is likely to emerge as a key stumbling block in future talks between the two sides, which agreed negotiations of a final peace settlement would resume within two months of the Hebron partial handover.
U.S. officials at the Erez border crossing where Netanyahu and Arafat met lit up cigars after the deal was clinched.
"I am very pleased to announce on behalf of the two leaders that they have reached an agreement," Ross told reporters as Netanyahu and Arafat emerged from their negotiations.
The right-wing Israeli leader and former Palestinian guerrilla chief shook hands but did not speak to reporters.
Ross said the agreement included a "note for the record" which dealt with future Israeli redeployments from the West Bank and other non-Hebron related issues.

"These two documents represent a very important building block in terms of developing the relations between the two sides and in terms of laying out a pathway of greater hope and the possibility for peace in the Middle East," he said.
Palestinian officials said Israelis and Palestinians spelled out commitments to each other in another section of the agreement titled "Agreed Minutes" but refused to disclose its contents.

Hebron, a West Bank flashpoint, is home to 400 militant Jewish settlers and 100,000 Arabs. It was due to be given self-rule 10 months ago but violence, security concerns and Israel's change of government in June delayed the pullback.
